item_name: Do connectome constraints improve task performance versus random or shuffled networks (null models, Beiran and Litwin-Kumar, others)

full_text_checked: Full text read: S1 Nature Neuroscience version via PMC (first about 100k of 153k characters: Results, Figs 1-8 descriptions, part of Methods; the remaining Methods and Extended Data legends were not read); S2 arXiv HTML v1 (all sections including Tables 1-3 and Limitations); S3 bioRxiv full-text HTML (main text and figure legends; supplementary figures not opened); S4 Europe PMC full-text XML (first 100k of 185k characters: Results, Discussion, robustness Methods; Supplementary Tables not opened); S7 bioRxiv PDF text (Abstract, Methods, Results). Abstract or listing only: S8 both papers, S9 both abstracts. S5 and S6 numbers come from the sibling results I2 and I1 in the same results folder (those agents read the full texts). No code was run.
task_and_output: S1: a 'teacher' RNN with known weights performs a task (N = 300 sparse excitatory/inhibitory network producing cycling oscillations of different durations, Fig. 1), or empirical connectome circuits (larval Drosophila premotor circuit, 178 neurons, forward/backward crawling sequences; adult Drosophila central complex, 153 neurons, heading-direction ring attractor; larval zebrafish hindbrain line-attractor integrator, Fig. 5). A 'student' with the same weights but unknown per-neuron gains and biases is trained to match the task readout and/or recorded activity of M neurons. Output: activity of unrecorded neurons; the question is prediction of activity, not better task performance. S2: flyvis core (45,669 cells, 1,513,231 edges, 734 trainable parameters) with a linear decoder from pooled central-cell activity to (cos theta, sin theta) of a MovingEdge direction; MSE. S3: flyvis optic-flow task (Sintel) exactly as in Lappalainen 2024; output optic flow; evaluation is the match of model T4/T5 tuning and flash responses to recordings. S4: untrained whole-brain LIF model (127,400 neurons); output: predicted spiking of neurons (e.g., motor neuron MN9) after activating gustatory or mechanosensory neurons; compared to optogenetics and behaviour. S7: Elman-type RNNs with topology from macaque/marmoset/human region-level connectomes; sequence-recall memory (MSE) and n-back memory (NLL, 3 classes). S8: echo state reservoir with fly lateral horn wiring; 'seeing double' multifunctionality task (reconstruct two attractors).
data_and_independent_videos: No natural video in any source. S1: simulated teacher activity; empirical connectomes (larval premotor, adult central complex, zebrafish hindbrain); train/test are trials of the same simulated system. S2: synthetic MovingEdge stimuli, batch of 12 stimuli x 269 frames on 721 hexals (6 angles x 2 intensities, speed 2.4); the paper does not describe a held-out stimulus split [uncertain]. S3: Sintel optic-flow sequences with the original flyvis train/validation split; two new ensembles of 50 models each. S4: no training data; predictions tested against published and new experiments (164 testable predictions; split-GAL4 screen over 106 cell types). S7: 1000 generated trials per task, 80% train, 20% test. S8: synthetic dynamical-system trajectories. Not applicable to 'independent videos'; none of the sources tests generalization to unseen natural videos.
target_size_and_input_resolution: S2 and S3 use the flyvis eye of 721 hexagonal columns (single grey channel). S2 stimulus is a full-field moving edge (no object target). S3 uses Sintel frames rendered onto the 721-hexal lattice as in Lappalainen 2024. S1, S4, S7, S8 have no visual input lattice (S4 stimulates sensory neurons directly at 10-260 Hz). No source involves a small target; target size is not applicable.
frame_rate_and_camera_motion: S2: 269 frames per MovingEdge stimulus at the flyvis integration step (dt not stated in what was read [uncertain]); no camera motion. S3: Sintel (rendered camera and object motion) at the flyvis Lappalainen setting. S1, S4, S7, S8: no video, continuous-time or discrete-time simulations. None tests a 30 Hz moving and rescaling crop.
detector_and_exemplar: No detector and no exemplar in any source. The 'target' in S1 is the activity of the teacher network; in S2 a direction label; in S3 the optic-flow field; in S4 experimentally measured neuron or behaviour responses.
trainable_nodes_and_loss: S1: student trains only per-neuron gains and biases (about 2N unknowns, connectome weights fixed); losses: MSE to the teacher readout, plus MSE to the M recorded neurons. Comparison student: 'unconstrained' student where weights are trained instead. S2: 734 flyvis parameters (2959 fixed) plus a linear decoder, Adam lr 1e-3, MSE, only 5 and 10 optimization steps. S3: flyvis training unchanged from Lappalainen 2024 (734 parameters plus flow decoder, flow endpoint loss). S4: nothing trained; one hand-calibrated global weight W_syn (set so that 100 Hz sugar-GRN activation gives about 80% of maximal MN9 firing). S7: all weights trained with backpropagation through time (Adam or RMSprop, lr 1e-4, ReLU or tanh, 500 epochs sequence task, 3000 epochs n-back). S8: reservoir fixed, linear readout trained (ridge, as usual for ESNs) [uncertain].
controls_seeds_splits: S1: connectome-constrained versus unconstrained students; random-parameter student before training (M = 0 error) as baseline; shuffled-identity baseline (comparing activity to randomly permuted teacher neurons); weight-noise and activation-mismatch perturbations (Fig. 4); optimal versus random choice of recorded neurons. No shuffled-connectome student is the main control; the key contrast is constrained versus unconstrained. S2 (most direct null-model study for flyvis): three graphs with identical node, edge and self-loop counts (connectome; naive random self-loop-matched graph; degree-preserving rewired graph by 250,000 accepted directed double-edge swaps, about 0.17 swaps per edge, acceptance 0.992, five samples); three stages: (A) both graphs started from a connectome-trained checkpoint, (B) both from a shared random initialization, (C) degree-preserving null from the same random initialization; seeds {0,1,2}; matched optimization steps (5 and 10), not wall-clock. Parameter sharing per cell type is inherited from flyvis metadata in all graphs (topology not fully separated from parameter sharing). S3: two independent retrained ensembles of 50 models with unchanged hyperparameters versus the published ensemble; alternative model-selection rules (Supplementary Figs 1b-3b). S4: shuffled-weight control (connection weights randomly shuffled, global weight distribution kept; 100 shuffles) for the MN9 sugar result only; parameter robustness sweeps (W_syn +/-30%, inhibitory:excitatory ratio +/-50%, glutamate sign flip). S5 (from sibling I2): 50-model ensemble; random-parameter DMNs with only the decoder trained; unconstrained CNNs (414,666 parameters, 5 models); synthetic sparse versus dense networks. S6 (from sibling I1): connectome init versus random init with connectome signs, with/without 40% noise, fixed versus trained weights, one run each. S7: each bio-instantiated network compared with the same network after shuffling its connection weights (same weight multiset, topology destroyed); 12 hyperparameter combinations x 5 runs. S8: Erdos-Renyi reservoir and rewired variants of the connectome.
metrics_and_numbers:
S2 (arXiv:2604.04033v1). Table 1 / Section 4.1: all graphs 45,669 nodes, 1,513,231 edges, 12,380 self-loops. Section 6.1, Figs 3-4 (checkpoint start, connectome vs naive random): loss 0.514 vs 0.698 at 5 steps, 0.499 vs 0.557 at 10 steps; mean absolute activity 0.656 vs 1.861 (5 steps), 0.740 vs 1.379 (10 steps); elapsed 252 vs 309 s (5), 546 vs 645 s (10). Table 2 (control minus connectome): checkpoint + naive random dLoss +0.1841 (5 steps), +0.0583 (10); shared random init + naive random dLoss -0.0020 (5), -0.0020 (10); shared random init + degree-preserving dLoss +0.0003 (5), -0.0018 (10); degree-preserving ensemble (5 samples x 3 seeds, 5 steps) dLoss +0.0017, dActivity -0.0108, dElapsed +10.72 s. Section 6.4: loss 0.5155 +/- 0.0067 (connectome) vs 0.5172 +/- 0.0061 (degree-preserving). Section 6.5: pre-training activity 0.5682 +/- 0.0059 vs 0.5774 +/- 0.0062 (1.64%, Section 7.5); gradient norms 9.75 +/- 4.21 vs 8.96 +/- 3.96. Small-world and ring-lattice nulls diverged (non-finite), Section 10. Interpretation: the apparent topology advantage (+0.184 loss) is an initialization artifact; under fair controls the difference is about 0.002 loss, within seed variation.
S1 (Nature Neuroscience 2025). Fig. 1: with readout-only training, students solve the task but do not match single-neuron activity. Fig. 2: for the N = 300 teacher, unrecorded-neuron error falls to the level of recorded neurons once about M* = 30 neurons are recorded; unconstrained students (weights trained) barely recover unrecorded activity even when most neurons are recorded. Fig. 3: required M scales with dimensionality, not N, for low-rank networks; chaotic networks need M growing with N (N = 400 needs M = 64; N = 1000 needs M = 256). Fig. 5: a handful of recorded neurons suffices for ring and line attractors, about 10 for larval premotor sequences. Optimal choice of 10 recorded neurons gives about 60% lower error than random choice (N = 300). Authors: a connectome 'often does not substantially constrain the dynamics of recurrent networks'. Task performance gain from the connectome is not measured.
S3 (bioRxiv 2026). Cluster mean validation task errors differ by less than 0.08 across the two retrained ensembles; in the original ensemble the lowest-error cluster matched measured T4c tuning (Fig. 1a-b), but in both retrained ensembles the lowest-error cluster did not reliably match recordings (Fig. 1c-f); the 'largest cluster in the top 20%' rule is post hoc. No correlation coefficient between task error and biological match given in what was read.
S4 (Nature 2024). 91% of 164 testable predictions matched experiments (Discussion; Supplementary Table 9); 84% excluding the split-GAL4 screen (Supplementary Table 10); >90% of 106 cell types correct at 50 Hz in the split-GAL4 screen (Fig. 2). Shuffled-weight control: MN9 activated in 100% of real-connectome simulations at 100 Hz sugar input versus 1 of 100 shuffled simulations (Results; Supplementary Table 1d). Robustness (Supplementary Table 11): W_syn +30% keeps 95% of predictions (accuracy 88%); W_syn -30% keeps 90.2% (accuracy 85%) [uncertain: wording in source ambiguous]; inhibition weakened/strengthened by 50% keeps 95%/96%; glutamate as excitatory raises optogenetic false positives from 1% to 16%.
S5 (from sibling I2, Lappalainen 2024 Extended Data Fig. 3): optic-flow EPE task-optimised DMNs 5.1-5.5, random-parameter DMNs with trained decoder about 5.7, unconstrained CNNs 4.5-4.6 (a.u.). So connectome-constrained models are worse at the task than an unconstrained CNN; the connectome's value is neural prediction (e.g., T4/T5 DSI task-optimised vs random p = 2e-11). S6 (from sibling I1, Tschopp 2018 Fig. 7, values read from bars): position error trained connectome about 2.0 ommatidia, random + 40% noise about 2.13, overlapping error bars; fixed connectome 2.6.
S7 (Goulas et al., Figs 3-5, Section 5.1): all construction strategies except 'weight mapping-equal' reach test loss comparable to the weight-shuffled random-topology controls on both memory tasks; abstract: 'no enhancement of performance when compared to randomly wired RNNs'. Exact loss values only in figures (not extracted).
S8 (abstract): fly lateral horn reservoir shows greater multifunctional capacity and a wider working spectral-radius range than Erdos-Renyi; numbers not extracted [uncertain].
tested_conditions: Unseen videos: no (no source uses natural video with a held-out video split; S3 uses Sintel validation as in flyvis). Target absence: no (not reported in any source). Similar distractors: no. Occlusion: no. Night or low light: no. Sequential operation on own predictions: no (S1 students are driven by teacher input; S7 tasks are open-loop). Out-of-distribution generalization: recommended but not done in S3; not reported elsewhere.
mechanism_summary: Published finding, in plain words: wiring alone does not make a network better at a task. (1) When connectome and random graphs are trained the same way from the same start, task loss is the same (S2: difference about 0.002 vs 0.184 when the connectome got a pre-trained start; S7: no gain over shuffled wiring; S6: random-init tracking network within error bars of connectome-init; S5: connectome networks lose to an unconstrained CNN on optic flow). (2) What the connectome does provide is a constraint that makes the internal activity of unrecorded neurons predictable, but only together with a small number of recordings (S1: about 30 of 300 neurons; few for attractor circuits), and only when training touches per-neuron parameters, not weights. (3) Even the biological match of flyvis is unstable across retrainings with identical task error (S3). (4) Untrained whole-brain models can make correct qualitative predictions, and these depend on the specific wiring (S4: 100/100 vs 1/100 for a shuffled control). Implication, not published: any claim that FlyVis causes a tracking gain must beat a same-topology-statistics null trained identically, not only a smaller MLP; the published literature gives no case where connectome topology improved an engineering task under fair controls.
transfer_limits: 1) No source uses natural video, a moving and rescaling crop, 30 Hz, or targets of about 9 x 12 lattice steps; S2 and S3 are the only ones on the 721-hexal flyvis eye and they use full-field edges or Sintel flow. 2) S2 trains for only 5-10 steps, 3 seeds, on one stimulus family; its null result is weak evidence for long training but its methodological point (checkpoint start creates a fake advantage) transfers fully: our D (trained FlyVis) starts from a Sintel-pretrained checkpoint, while B (no FlyVis, ~9,602 parameters) starts from scratch, so D vs B mixes pretraining, topology and parameter count. 3) S2's nulls keep per-type parameter sharing; a rewired flyvis also keeps 734 parameters, so it controls parameter count but not 'cell-type identity'. Rewired graphs without retraining are broken circuits (sibling I2 F1 v2: 0.857 -> 0.539 accuracy), which tests damage, not topology. 4) S1 applies to predicting neural activity; we have no recordings, so its main positive result (recordings remove degeneracy) does not apply to a tracker. 5) S4 is untrained and deterministic sensorimotor routing, unrelated to visual tracking. 6) S7 and S8 use non-fly or non-visual connectomes and different training (BPTT on macro-connectomes; reservoirs), so only the sign of the null result transfers. 7) Our environment (YOLO26s, ByteTrack, MASA) dominates HOTA; previous FlyVis variant changed HOTA by +0.0087 [-0.0299; +0.0561], so any null-model comparison needs the paired per-video bootstrap and probably a more sensitive intermediate metric (useful-center rate in paired continuation) before HOTA. 8) Re-selection along a 50-model ensemble (S3) means the chosen FlyVis model (flow/0000/000) is one of many with similar task error; differences between ensemble members are an additional nuisance factor to sample.
research_questions_addressed: Q2 (direct, methodological): S2 shows how initialization and null choice create or remove an apparent connectome advantage; S1 shows connectome-constrained versus unconstrained parameterizations have different solution spaces; S3 shows that equal task error hides different internal solutions. Together they say: separate representation from readout by training identical readouts on (a) stock FlyVis, (b) FlyVis at random prior parameters, (c) degree-preserving rewired FlyVis retrained identically, (d) receptors-only input. Q5 (direct, design): defines the matched controls needed to attribute a tracking benefit to FlyVis rather than readout, extra training or compute: same observations and history, same readout and its parameter count, same optimizer steps and seeds, same initialization protocol (both from scratch or both from equally pretrained checkpoints), same compute, and a degree-preserving null at equal core parameter count. Q1 and Q3: caution only; no source tests target selection, refusal or small targets. Q4: not addressed.
candidate_node_change: Not a new node but a mandatory control for any core node change (core, dynamics, connectivity). Proposed control set for the Z13 readout/core experiment, all with the identical exemplar of 4 last observations, the same crops, the same history, the same readout (~11,746 parameters), the same number of optimizer steps, the same 3+ seeds, and the same data split: (1) B: readout on receptors only (no FlyVis core, matched parameters by padding the readout); (2) C0: FlyVis core at random prior parameters, frozen (Lappalainen random-DMN control); (3) C: stock FlyVis flow/0000/000 frozen; (4) R: degree-preserving rewired FlyVis graph (directed double-edge swaps preserving per-cell in/out degree, ideally within cell-type pairs, about 0.17 swaps per edge as in S2), pretrained on Sintel with the same steps and schedule as stock FlyVis, then frozen; (5) D and D_R: (3) and (4) with the core trained on the object objective with the same steps; (6) a second stock ensemble member (e.g., flow/0000/001) to measure between-model variance (S3). Minimal check (cheap first): C0 vs C vs B on the existing paired-continuation useful-center metric, 3 seeds, no Sintel retraining; only if C beats both C0 and B with a paired bootstrap CI excluding zero, build R (Sintel pretraining of a rewired graph costs GPU hours; ask the author). Claim rule: 'FlyVis connectivity helps' requires C > R and D > D_R; 'FlyVis pretraining helps' requires C > C0; 'it is just the extra network' if B, C0 and C are equal. Stop condition: if C - C0 and C - B CIs both include zero after 3 seeds on the full dev set, record that the FlyVis representation adds nothing for Z13 and do not run R; if C > C0 but R matches C, record a pretraining (not connectome) effect.
strongest_objection: The most direct flyvis null-model study (S2) is a single-author preprint with only 5-10 optimization steps, 3 seeds and one synthetic task; a topology advantage could appear only after full training or on natural video, so 'no advantage' is not proven. Conversely, the only positive results (S4 shuffled control, S8 reservoirs) concern untrained or reservoir networks and qualitative routing, not trained task performance. So the literature neither shows nor rules out a connectome benefit for tracking; it shows only that naive controls (checkpoint versus scratch, unequal pretraining, naive random graphs) manufacture advantages. Our existing B/C/D comparisons have exactly this confound, so earlier positive FlyVis signs in the project cannot be attributed to connectivity.
evidence_strength: S1: peer-reviewed (Nature Neuroscience 2025), code public; strong for the activity-prediction claim, not about task performance. S4: peer-reviewed (Nature 2024), code public, experimentally validated; strong for its routing predictions, one shuffle control only. S5/S6: peer-reviewed / preprint, see I2/I1. S2: preprint, single author, no linked code, short training; weak-to-moderate, but methodologically clear and consistent with S5-S7. S3: preprint, code public; moderate. S7: preprint/workshop, code public; moderate for a null result on macro-connectomes. S8: preprint and journal paper, abstract only; weak here. Overall: moderate evidence that connectome topology gives no task-performance advantage under fair controls; no independent replication of a positive task advantage exists.
